prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: chasing a contractor for repairs. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the repair contractor goes quiet after the initial survey, I should send a short written chaser and ask for a fresh target date rather than assuming the job is still progressing."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a contractor has promised a date more than once, I should treat the latest missed date as a risk signal and escalate to a manager or alternative supplier if there is no same-day response."},{"type":"observation","content":"When chasing repairs, I get a quicker reply if I include the claim reference, the outstanding action, and the exact information needed, because vague chasers tend to be ignored."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the member is being kept waiting for repair updates, I prefer to copy them into the next chaser or give them a clear summary, so they know the claim is still being actively managed."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a contractor says they are waiting on parts or materials, I should ask for the specific item and an estimated lead time, because 'awaiting parts' can hide a lack of progress."},{"type":"fact","content":"When repairs are urgent for habitability or security, I should not let repeated chasing delay the next practical step, such as approving a temporary fix or arranging an alternative contractor."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a contractor is difficult to reach, I should try a different contact route and record each attempt, because a clear contact trail makes later escalation much easier."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I need a prompt response, I prefer to set a deadline in plain terms, such as 'please confirm by 3 pm tomorrow', instead of using open-ended wording."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the repair scope is changing, I should ask the contractor to confirm what is included and what is excluded before chasing completion, because uncertainty over scope causes avoidable back-and-forth."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there has been no meaningful progress after several chasers, I should stop relying on reassurance and move to a formal escalation or supplier replacement to protect the member’s experience."}]}
